introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. English Language 2 (0730), June 2019, ADVANCED LEVEL. Paper 2: Section A - Summary and Text Reconstruction; Section B - Composition; Section C - Prescribed Texts. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Answer BOTH questions in SECTION A and ONE EACH from SECTIONS B and C in the SAME Answer Booklet, beginning each section on a new page. Begin with SECTION A.

Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks.

Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure considered as an attempt to cheat will earn you a penalty.

In the SUMMARY question, use mainly your own words. Indiscriminate copying of portions of the passage as your answer will earn you no marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

A pre-prepared or memorized composition will earn you no marks.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**SECTION B - COMPOSITION (20 marks)**

Mark distribution: Content and Organisation (06 marks); Expression (08 marks); Accuracy (06 marks).

Choose ONE topic to write about from the list below. You are advised to write clearly and effectively, to spell and punctuate correctly, and to ensure that your writing is appropriate in style and content to the topic chosen. Avoid obscene language and do not disclose your identity. You should write between 500 and 550 words.

questions.corrige_markdown:
**Plan**

1. Introduction: definition and scope of migration.
2. Types: internal, international, voluntary and forced.
3. Causes: push and pull factors.
4. Advantages, then disadvantages.
5. Solutions and conclusion.

**Model composition (531 words)**

Migration, the movement of people from one place to another in search of a better life, is as old as humanity itself. From the herders who follow their cattle across the Sahel to the graduates who queue at foreign embassies in Yaounde, people have always left the places of their birth when those places could no longer satisfy their needs. Today the phenomenon has reached unprecedented levels, and it raises questions that no society can afford to ignore.

Migration takes several forms. Internal migration, such as the drift of young villagers from the grassfields to Douala or Yaounde, is the most common in our country. International migration carries people across borders, whether toward neighbouring states or toward Europe and North America. Some migrants leave by choice, hoping for a higher income or a better education; others are forced to flee from war, famine or persecution.

The causes are usually explained in terms of "push" and "pull" factors. Poverty, unemployment, poor schools and hospitals, insecurity and the decline of rural farming push people out of their villages. At the same time, the bright lights of the city, the promise of well-paid jobs and the glowing stories told by returning relatives pull them toward distant places. Television and the internet have magnified this attraction by presenting the wealthy world as an easy paradise.

Migration brings undeniable benefits. Migrants send money home, and these remittances pay school fees, build houses and finance small businesses, often exceeding the foreign aid that reaches poor communities. Migrants also acquire new skills and ideas which they may later bring back, and the meeting of cultures enriches host societies. Moreover, emigration relieves pressure on overcrowded labour markets at home.

Yet the costs are heavy. Cities swell beyond the capacity of their water, housing and transport systems, giving rise to slums, crime and unemployment, while villages are left with the old and the very young, and their farms are abandoned. The departure of doctors, engineers and teachers deprives the home country of the very people it has trained at great expense. Irregular migrants risk their lives in the desert and on the Mediterranean Sea, and those who arrive may suffer exploitation, racism and loneliness. Families are separated for years, and children grow up without one or both parents.

If the problem is to be managed, its roots must be addressed. Governments should invest in rural roads, electricity, markets and agricultural credit so that farming can again offer a decent living. They should create jobs for the young, reward merit fairly and fight corruption, which convinces talented citizens that their future lies elsewhere. At the international level, wealthy countries and African states ought to cooperate on legal channels of migration, student exchanges and fair labour contracts, instead of building walls and ignoring the smugglers who profit from despair.

In conclusion, migration is neither a curse nor a blessing in itself. It is a natural human response to inequality, and it will continue as long as opportunity is unevenly distributed. The wise course is not to forbid people from leaving but to make staying a real choice, and to ensure that those who go can do so safely, lawfully and with dignity.

**Marking grid**

| Criterion | Marks | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Content and Organisation | 6 | Relevant ideas that answer the topic, developed with examples, in clear paragraphs with an introduction and a conclusion |
| Expression | 8 | Varied vocabulary and sentence structures, appropriate style and tone, fluent links between ideas |
| Accuracy | 6 | Correct grammar, tenses, spelling and punctuation |

**Common mistakes**

1. Treating the topic as a story or a personal experience instead of a balanced discussion with causes, effects and solutions.
2. General statements with no examples, and paragraphs that mix several ideas.

incertitudes: Consigne de la page de garde (règle de choix) : « Answer BOTH questions in SECTION A and ONE EACH from SECTIONS B and C in the SAME Answer Booklet ». Section A obligatoire (aucune règle), Section B : 1 sujet sur 6 (a à f), Section C : 1 question sur 4. Les regles_choix sont identiques dans les 12 fichiers.

Fautes imprimées dans le sujet, laissées telles quelles : titre « SECTION A SUMMERY AND TEXT RECONSTRUCTION » (summary), « for few hours » (Q1), « A this stage », « into the will » (mill), « The stripped cane are then », « out of them » (Q2, forme reconstruite) ; Section C question 2 : « Use any Three prescribed text ».
Le tiret cadratin du passage de résumé (« choice of home - among the stinging tentacles ») est écrit « - » conformément à la règle du projet. Le passage ne porte pas de numéros de ligne imprimés.

Section A : le sujet imprime 30 marks pour la section (15 par question). La répartition des 15 points du résumé n'est pas imprimée : la grille du corrigé est indicative. La reconstruction est comptée à 1 point par blanc (15 blancs), ce qui est une hypothèse ; plusieurs réponses sont acceptables pour certains blancs (voir le corrigé).

Section B : 20 marks (Content and Organisation 6, Expression 8, Accuracy 6), 500 à 550 mots demandés. Points imprimés non corrigés. Compositions modèles : comptes de mots faits par script (de 517 à 534 mots).
